transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Iran says it met with a U.S. delegation on the sidelines of the United Nations General
Assembly and that Qatar served as the mediator.
This meeting followed President Trump's address to the U.N. body.
That's where he threatened that he could, quote, "annihilate Iran if a deal is not reached."
And Piers Hadil al-Shalchi has more.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Bakhai called the meeting with the U.S. "an
interaction" used to convey Iran's conditions, according to Iranian state media.
Those conditions, he said, included halting of U.S. hostilities, an end to the U.S. naval
blockade and the release of Iranian funds.
President Trump said earlier Tuesday that U.S. envoys met with Iranian officials for
three hours.
He said Iran must decide whether it will agree to a deal or face, quote, "obliteration."
The U.S. special envoy, Steve Witkoff, who has been leading talks with Iran, said he
felt, quote, "very good" following the meeting.
Hadil al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping is now heading toward the United States.
It's his first state visit to the U.S. in more than a decade.
And Piers Jennifer Pack reports from Beijing.
President Xi heads to Washington with Taiwan trade and tech expected to be high on his agenda.
The last time Xi met Trump in May, they agreed to more stability.
American studies scholar Wu Xingbo at Shanghai's Fudan University says it was the warmest he's
seen U.S.-China relations in years.
But since then, he says, things have been fragile.
In the last several months, the U.S. had continued to contain and pressure China.
Like imposing extra tariffs, blacklisting more Chinese firms, and banning new imports
of Chinese humanoid robots.
This visit then, says Wu, is more about building mutual trust.
Jennifer Pack, NPR News, Beijing.
The Trump administration is canceling the health insurance for 760,000 phantom enrollees
on healthcare.gov.
And Piers Selina Simmons-Duffin reports the government is providing few details about
how it determined the health plans were not legitimate.
Trump administration officials explained in a press conference that they suspected fraudster
brokers had signed up people who weren't eligible or who didn't even know they had
been signed up.
The fight against fraudulent brokers has been going on for years, says Cynthia Cox of the
nonprofit health research organization KFF, but she questioned this approach.
There could have been collateral damage here.
If someone didn't file a claim, she points out, they might have just been healthy.
And if they didn't respond to the notice in time, they might have just missed it.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services did not respond to NPR's questions by airtime
about what happens if there were mistakes and people had their plans canceled in error.
Selina Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The Justice Department has unsealed an indictment against a former U.S. postal worker.
It accuses him of throwing out about 300 mail ballots that were intended for people casting
ballots in Utah's June primary election.
Officials say that the suspect told authorities in Utah he threw the ballots and other mail
into a church dumpster.
That was because he wanted to lighten his workload, he said, not because of a political
reason.
The U.S. military says an F-16 fighter jet crashed yesterday in Germany.
The pilot sustained injuries after ejecting from the aircraft.
Officials at the U.S. Air Base in western Germany say the cause of the jet crash is being investigated.
Voting is now open for Fat Bear Week.
The annual competition features the chunky brown bears of Alaska's Katmai National Park
and Preserve.
It draws fans from around the world.
Alaska Public Media's Ava White reports.
A fat bear is a successful bear, and the 16 contenders are really chubby.
Fat Bear Week celebrates how much weight the animals pack on for feasting on massive sockeye
salmon runs.
The bears are relatable to fans voting in the competition, like Linden Norman in northwest
Arkansas.
And I think that people can kind of find some inspiration from their resiliency, and it's
just wholesome.
And it's bears doing what they want to do, getting fat.
You can vote for your favorite fat bear at fatbearweek.org through September 29th when
a weighty winner will be crowned.
For NPR News, I'm Ava White in Anchorage.
And I'm Cora Vekulman, NPR News in Washington.
This week and up first, we talk about the economy.
Trucks, trains, and tractors run on diesel, which is now priced at record highs, with
less than 50 days until the midterm elections.
So the next six weeks are going to be intense.
Let Up First get you through it one morning at a time with three stories you need to know
each day.
Listen to Up First on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
